newsitem.title: USA: Clinton borrows from Bush in seeking a legacy.
newsitem.headline: Clinton borrows from Bush in seeking a legacy.

text.p: Foiled in his first term bid to reform the U.S. health care system, Bill Clinton now wants to go down in history as the "Education President" -- the same legacy former President George Bush thirsted for.
As Republican Bush discovered, it may be easier for Democrat Clinton to talk about improving the nation's schools than do it.

Declaring that high standards of learning are essential if the United States is to compete in the "knowledge economy" of the 21st Century, the president said on Tuesday night his top priority over the next four years "is to ensure that Americans have the best education in the world."

"We must begin a national crusade for education standards -- not federal government standards, but national standards representing what all of our children must know," Clinton said in his State of the Union speech. "Every state and every school must shape the curriculum to reflect these standards, and train teachers to lift students up to meet them."

The need to strengthen U.S. education has been a subject of intense discussion since Ronald Reagan's presidency in the 1980s, when a national commission found a "rising tide of mediocrity" in American schools, and warned that the country faced inevitable decline if the situation were not reversed.
Bush was then vice president and later tried to make the issue his own with indifferent success." Now comes Clinton.

At the heart of his 10-point "Call to Action" is a plan to encourage school districts to participate in national achievement tests in 4th grade reading and 8th grade math to make sure children master the basics.

He proposed $51 billion for education in the budget year beginning next Oct. 1, a 20 percent increase over current spending, to pay for education, training and tax cuts tied to education. Under his programme spending would rise to nearly $60 billion a year by 2002 even as other programmes are cut to balance the federal budget by that year.

"This is roughly double the size of the commitment that (former President) Lyndon Johnson made when the federal government first began its investment in this area," in the mid-1960s, budget director Franklin Raines told reporters.

Clinton has said he would like to be remembered as a progressive peace-time president in the same league as Theodore Roosevelt, who helped transform the United States from an agricultural to an industrial society.
As Arkansas governor, Clinton co-chaired an advisory panel that made recommendations to then-President Bush on how to fix the education system. But many were never implemented.

"Traditionally, the teachers unions have opposed real reform and greater parental involvement, and that spells trouble for what the president says he wants to do" said Karen Miller of the conservative Heritage Foundation, noting that Clinton's Democratic Party has strong links to the National Education Association and American Federation of Teachers.
"It's good for President Clinton to be discussing this, but he should be talking about things like school choice if he's going to truly transform the education system in this country," Miller said.
Clinton opposes a Republican plan to issue vouchers to parents to allow them to send their children to schools of their choice, saying this would undermine public education.

And if former Clinton political consultant Dick Morris is to be believed, the president's call for voluntary student achievement tests -- first proposed in a 1996 speech to U.S. state governors -- represents a poll-tested "cop-out."
Morris resigned from the Clinton re-election campaign in disgrace last August after being caught in a sex scandal involving a prostitute.

"The president really wanted to require states to pass such tests, but found that there wasn't the base of public support for such enforcement. So we confined ourselves to usging states to adopt testing requirements," Morris writes in his new book on Clinton's quest for a second term, "Behind the Oval Office."
